localChanges: Civilization II games now run Civilization II's cities: shield waste and the link to your capital, Entertainers only below size 5, plunder and Partisans when a city falls, Farmland with the Supermarket, Capitalization, the penalty for changing what a city builds, Auto build, rapture growth, Leonardo's Workshop, Nuclear Plant meltdowns and the Apollo Program's revealed map (#1007).

In Civilization II games, a city's citizens can now be angry, and the city screen and the Happiness report show Civilization II's stages of happiness: the base, luxuries, buildings, martial law and units, and Wonders (#1007).

In Civilization II games, the production list warns how many shields a change would lose, counts the turns from what would be left, and shows Capitalization as gold per turn; a city can be put on Auto for units only or improvements only (#1007).

In Civilization II games, the map, the square tooltip and the city screen show what each square yields the city working it, with its Harbor, Supermarket, Colossus or celebration, and a city of Entertainers below size 5 no longer offers to change them (#1007).

With Civilization II's art imported, cities are drawn in the industrial and modern styles as their civilization advances, at Civilization II's sizes, with the capital a size larger; import PEOPLE.GIF as well for Civilization II's citizens. On the isometric map, cities now change sprite at Civilization II's sizes, in Civilization games too (#1007).

In Civilization II games, you're now told when your units are upgraded, when a captured city's treasury is plundered, when Partisans rise, when a Nuclear Plant melts down, when the Apollo Program reveals the world and when a celebrating city grows, and you're asked whether to move your Palace when your capital falls (#1007).

Choosing which squares a city works now weighs what each square gives that city (City#tileYields), so a ruleset's square-by-square bonuses count when citizens are placed. With no such rule, squares are weighed as before.

A new SpecialistAvailable rule says which kinds of specialist a city may have. Making, cycling and removing specialists only use the kinds the city may have. With no rule, every kind is available, as before.

The worked-tiles yield rule asks the city what each square gives it, so a CityTileYield rule would apply. Civ1 registers none, so nothing changes in play.

So seams that ask about a city can use the game's own rules when no registry is passed.

A new CityTileYield rule changes one worked square's yields in the context of its city, for bonuses and penalties a ruleset applies square by square. City#tileYields(tile) gives a square's yields for the city with those rules applied, and City#tileYieldRules() fetches the rules once for a pass over many squares. With no rule registered it returns the tile's own yields, unchanged.

Re-pricing a build or clearing its queue, as a capture does when the city keeps what it was building, now forgets the turn's starting production, so the new owner can't get the old owner's production back by changing to the original item.

The progress a city had at the start of the turn is forgotten when its build is cancelled or cleared, as on a capture, and once anything else sets its progress, so a new owner's choice is never worked out from the old owner's production.
Changing back to the item the turn started with restores the production it had then, even when the rule gives no answer.
A new BuildOverflow rule says how much production a completed item leaves for the next one. With none, a completed item's production still goes back to 0.
A new BuildCategory rule puts each buildable item in a category of the ruleset's own, which lib/buildCategory gives.

A new ProductionChanged rule says how much production a city keeps when it changes what it builds. It is asked from what the city had at the start of the turn, so changing back in the same turn gives the production back. With none, a change keeps the production, as before, and nothing new is saved.

lib/assignWorkers now re-exports base-city-lifecycle's, so everything that places citizens through library-city weighs squares by what they give the city and respects which specialists a city may have.
Its workflow now installs with pnpm and runs the tests.

In Civ2, where a city's buildings and government change what a square gives it, computer players judge each square by what it gives that city, when choosing which citizens to make Entertainers and when weighing The Republic.

A computer player's city builds Capitalization only when nothing else is worth building, rather than because it costs nothing, and at the start of each turn a city on Capitalization chooses again, so it builds something as soon as something is worth building.

In Civ2, which takes shields when a city changes what it builds, a computer player's city part of the way through a build doesn't change to anything that would lose them, unless an enemy is next to it or it needs a defender, and it doesn't switch to a Temple or the like to calm disorder if that would lose them either.
Computer players' workers build Farmland on the irrigated squares a city works once it has, or is building, a Supermarket, where they can build it, and don't dig a mine over Farmland.

In Civ2, a computer player's city that was in civil disorder at the start of its turn now builds a Temple or the like and hurries it, even if it was calmed during the turn, and the player raises luxuries for cities in disorder or on the edge of it, judged by Civ2's own rules and angry citizens. Civ1 games are unchanged.
